line:
"Good morning, Mother Aldith. I'm Brannoc Ashdown, Edda Thorne's foster-son, and I've come with two matters. A boy named Tobin has a crushed ankle at Brother Ansel's hospice, and a dyer in Greywater, Perrin Gale, has a hip that healed crooked after a fall from a rack."

I hold out the note. "This is also from me, for a dyer's daughter named Wren, twelve, who sweeps the chapel there and wants to learn the work. Maud Marrow vouches for her, and her parents have agreed to a month's trial. Will you read it, and will you see Tobin today?"

entries.text:
Aldith doesn't stop kneading. She jerks her chin at the table, and you set the note down on the one clean corner. She wipes her hands on her apron, one finger at a time, then picks it up and reads it with her lips pressed thin.

"Edda Thorne's boy," she says. "I met Edda once, thirty years back. She told me I was too loud for a sickroom. I told her she was too soft for a bone." A grunt that might be a laugh. "Maud Marrow vouches for the girl? Maud's blankets have kept my feet warm eleven winters, so that counts for something. A dyer's child with a steady hand and a chapel broom. Hm."

She folds the note into her apron pocket. "A month's trial, and the parents can fetch her home at harvest? That's sensible. I don't take a child who's been shipped to me like a sack of meal. Tell her to come with Maud when the roads are dry, and I'll find out whether she faints at the sight of a bone."

Then she looks at you properly. "Tobin. Crushed, you say, and not set? Don't tell me you've been pushing healing prayers into it. Magic closes a bone any way it likes, and then I have to break it again." She wipes her hands again, harder. "Has anyone touched that ankle but you and Ansel?"

On Perrin's hip, her face closes up. "A month healed crooked, and a hip, not a wrist. That's a hard, ugly job, and he'd have to come to me. I'm not walking to Greywater with my saws. If the old fool will make the journey, tell him to bring a cart and a bottle."

She is waiting for your answer about the ankle. It is a little past half past six on Day 6.

entries.text: notebook: updated Mother Aldith

Aldith keeps kneading while you speak. At "Edda Thorne" her hands slow, and at "foster-son" they stop. She wipes them on her apron, takes the note and reads it at arm's length, lips moving. It is short, and she reads it twice.

"Edda's boy. She wrote me once, forty years back, to tell me I set a wrist like a butcher." She grunts, almost fondly. "She was right. I've set it better since."

She folds the note into her apron. "The boy first. Crushed, you say? Have Ansel's lad carry him here on a litter, and keep him still on the way. I'll have my table ready. A crush heals worse for being left, so I'll see him within the hour."

Then she squints at you. "The dyer's hip is another thing. A hip healed crooked has to be broken and set again, and I won't do that by letter or on hearsay. He comes to me himself, and he pays what he can, which is more than he'll want to. Tell him Aldith says a crooked man walks twice as far as a straight one." She sniffs. "The girl I'll look at when she stands in my door with Maud Marrow at her back. A month's trial, is it? Sensible parents. Most prentices come with none. If she can stomach blood and doesn't faint at a snapped bone, we'll talk."

She jerks her chin at the bench by the wall. "Sit, if you've time. Tell me how that hip looked, which side, and how high. And what you did for it. I'd hear it from the hands that touched it."

It's a little before seven on Day 6. Tobin is waiting on a litter, the town is waking, and you have two 1st-level slots left.

entries.text: notebook: updated Mother Aldith

Aldith keeps kneading while you speak. She doesn't interrupt, and she doesn't look up until you hold out the note. Then she wipes her hands on her apron, takes it between a floury finger and thumb, and reads it with her lips pressed thin.

"Edda Thorne's foster-son," she says. "Edda once told me I set bones like a butcher with a grudge. She was right, and it works." She grunts. "Tobin first. A crushed ankle in a nine-year-old can't wait. I'll be at Ansel's before the bread is out of the oven. Tell him to have the boy fed and the bed clear, and to keep the child from his own mother's panic, if he's got one."

She taps the note against the table. "A dyer's girl who sweeps a priestless chapel unasked. Hm. I've had three apprentices, and two stayed. The ones who stay are the ones nobody had to ask. Maud Marrow's word is good, and I owe her a blanket's worth of favours. Send the girl down with Maud when the weather holds, and I'll look at her hands before I look at anything else. I promise nothing past that. A month's trial suits me. A year's would suit me better."

On Perrin she is less gentle. "A hip that's healed crooked a month? I can break it and set it again, and it will hurt him worse than the fall did. I'm not walking two days to do it. If the old fool wants it straight, he comes to me, on a cart, with someone to hold his hand. Tell him that. Tell him Aldith says pride is a bad splint."

She jerks her chin at the door. "Go on. I'll bring my own splints."

It is a little before seven on Day 6. You have two 1st-level slots, Channel Divinity ready, and 800 of the 900 XP you need. Tobin is in good hands, Perrin's road is plain, and Wren's is as open as you can make it.

input.add_to_description: Day 6 morning: Brannoc spoke for Wren and Perrin Gale. Aldith (heavy, sixty, forearms like a smith's, floury hands) will see Tobin today. She is unconvinced about Wren: won't promise to take her, but will see the girl herself when Maud brings her, and judge by her hands, not letters. She wants Perrin brought to her. entries.text: notebook: updated Mother Aldith

Aldith wipes one floury hand on her apron, takes the note, and reads it at arm's length with her lips pressed thin. She reads it twice, once for the words and once, you suspect, for the hand that wrote them.

"Edda's boy," she says. "She sent me a lad once with a broken wrist and a lecture. I set it and ignored the lecture." She sniffs. "Tobin first, because he's here and children's bones don't wait. Bring him on the litter and I'll have the table cleared. Crushed, you say? How crushed? Grip or weight?"

You tell her about the cart, the swelling, and the four gray marks round the ankle. She goes quiet at that last, and her eyes flick to the door. "Aye. Ansel's boy told me last night. Keep that to yourself in the market. Folk panic."

Then the note. Your Persuasion (8) doesn't move her far. She tucks the paper into her apron and shakes her head. "I've had three apprentices, and two stayed, and I buried my patience with the third. A letter's not a pair of hands. Maud Marrow's blankets keep my feet warm, and I'll not insult her by saying no outright. Bring the girl when the weather holds, and I'll see her hands work, one day, before I say yes or no. No promises." She jabs a finger at you. "And no lecture from you about it either."

On Perrin she is blunter. A month-old hip, healed crooked, is a hard business. She would have to break it again, and he would be abed for weeks. She'll not do it unless he walks the road to her door himself and asks. "Tell him a stool at the vat is sense, and that the rest is his to choose."

It is twenty to seven on Day 6. Tobin is still at the hospice, and Aldith is already shoving the dough aside to clear her table. You have two 1st-level slots, Channel Divinity, and 100 XP to go. Rudd, Imma and the bridge are all quiet.

Jory's skiff is drawn up on the mud at the south tip, empty, with the lantern gone and a coil of rope left. entries.text: notebook: updated Hollow Isle

You take the rope, the hooded lantern, three flasks, and your shield, and Wick and Gorm pole the skiff out through the channels in the thin afternoon light. Wick knows every turn. The mist is a pale skin on the water, the reeds hiss, and a heron lifts and flaps away ahead of you. You keep your talk low. By a little before half past four the Isle rises ahead, a low grey hump with the cut swathe raw at its tip.

Perception (17): you keep to the water, and a skiff lies drawn up on the mud at the south tip. It is Jory's, with the lantern gone and a coil of rope left in the bow. Two sets of prints lead up from it toward the mound's west flank. One is a boot, dragging, and the other is a smaller print, barefoot, small and narrow, a child's or a slight woman's. Neither pair comes back. The three Wick-fires hang low over the west side and do not stir. Nothing moves on the Isle, and it is utterly quiet. The reeds near the cut are grey as ash.

input.add_to_description: Day 14 ~4:30 PM: Scouted from skiff with Wick Hale and Gorm. Jory's skiff was not seen by Brannoc (Perception 10), though it lies drawn up among cut reeds on the south tip's far side. The Wick-fires held still and did not drift. Trip took 1 hr 35 min round.

entries.text: notebook: updated Hollow Isle

Wick Hale poles with the long unhurried strokes of a man born to it, and Gorm sits in the bow with an eel-spear. You sit amidships with the rope coiled at your feet, the hooded lantern shuttered, three flasks of oil in your lap, and your shield across your knees. The mist closes round you almost at once. The water is black and still, and the reeds hiss on both sides.

At the south tip Wick holds the skiff a long spear's length off the raw swathe of cut reeds. Perception (10): you see the bow-mark in the mud, the stumps, and a scatter of dropped reed-bundles, rotted brown. You can't see a skiff. The tall reeds on the tip's far side hide whatever lies there, and the mist is thick. Nothing says Jory is alive, and nothing says he is not.

The Wick-fires hold their places over the west flank, three pale green-white glows, perfectly still. They do not drift toward you, and you are glad. The air is cold and smells of grave-earth and wet stone. Wick's jaw is tight. Gorm says the reeds were never grey before. You stay a quarter of an hour, as you meant to, and turn back at half past four, as you said.

It is half past five on Day 14 when the skiff scrapes the staithe again, and dusk is on you. Ode is waiting on the landing with a lantern. You have four 1st-level slots, no 2nd-level slots, and Channel Divinity. The Isle is unsealed and a young man may be alive in it. Your next long rest could finish by half past three tomorrow afternoon, if you start now.

input.add_to_description: Day 14 ~4:40 PM: Scouted from skiff with Wick Hale and Gorm. Jory's skiff is drawn up in the cut reeds at the south tip, empty, its lantern gone, one eel-spear left in the bow, and a dark smear on the thwart (dried blood, not much). A trail of trampled reeds and a dragged heel-line run from it up the bank toward the west flank, ending at the sunken door. Wick-fires held still.

entries.text: notebook: updated Hollow Isle

The skiff slides out through the reeds with Wick poling at the stern and Gorm in the bow. You sit amidships with rope, the hooded lantern, and six flasks at your feet. The water is black and still, the mist is thin, and nobody speaks. Wick reads the channels without looking down, the way you read a hymn you have sung a thousand times. It takes the better part of an hour.

At the south tip you hold the skiff off thirty paces and look. Perception (16): the raw swathe of cut reeds is plain, and in it, drawn up in the stubble, lies a second skiff, empty. It is Jory's. His lantern is gone. One eel-spear lies in the bow, and there's a dark smear on the thwart, dried to brown. It's blood, but not much. A trail of trampled reed and a long heel-drag line run from the boat up the bank toward the west flank, and end at the sunken door you saw from the landing. Your Medicine tells you that a man dragged by the heels is a man who couldn't walk, and not necessarily a dead one.

The Wick-fires hold still on the far side, three pale glows low over the west flank, steady in the thickening dusk. They don't come nearer. Wick mutters, "Enough," and Gorm is already looking at you. The light is going.

It's twenty-five past five on Day 14, and you decide how to leave. You have four 1st-level slots, no 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and the rope. The sunken door is a hundred paces round the island. Jory may still be alive in the dark behind it.

Perception 10: a skiff's prow shows in the reeds near the cut swathe, but he could not tell if it is Jory's, nor see a mooring line or footprints. The air near the Isle is noticeably cold, and a smell of grave-earth lingers. The party withdrew at dusk.

entries.text: notebook: updated Hollow Isle

You load the skiff with rope, the hooded lantern, and a few flasks, and settle yourself amidships. Wick Hale takes the pole and Gorm the bow. The channel is narrow, and the reeds close in hissing on either side. Wick guides the boat with small sure thrusts. The village shrinks behind you into the mist.

As you near the Isle, the air grows cold, a flat, still cold that has no wind in it and smells of wet earth. Nobody speaks. At the south tip you hold the skiff in the reeds, thirty paces off, and look.

Perception (10): the cut swathe is raw and plain, with stubble and the trampled mud of the cutters' work. In the reeds just beyond it, something pale juts from the water that might be a prow. It might be a skiff drawn up and abandoned, or a drift-log. You can't tell. You can see no mooring line, no footprints you can read, and no sign of a person. The Wick-fires stay where they were, over the west side, three pale glows hanging unmoving in the grey. They don't stir toward you.

Gorm whispers that it's Jory's boat. Wick says it's a log. Neither knows.

You keep your word. You turn back well before dark, and nobody lands. The pole drips, the reeds hiss, and the village's few lights come up out of the mist. You are back at the staithe at half past five on Day 14, the light going. Ode is waiting on the planks with her arms folded.

You have four 1st-level slots, no 2nd-level slots, and Channel Divinity. The long rest from this afternoon has already counted, so you can't take another before half past three tomorrow. The Isle is a mile off, the Wick-fires are steady, and Jory has been gone five nights.
